headline: A researcher showed that AI agents that trust one another can be tricked into passing a hacker's instructions along through the MCP standard that links them.
score_reason: Pool score kept: named researcher, named vendors and fixes; it is proof-of-concept work and another expert says the attack is not new.
importance_line: Organisations that connect AI agents with MCP, and the people whose data those agents can reach, face a way for attackers to move between internal systems, and Ars argues that firms rushing to build agents have dropped the 'zero trust' principle (assume any part of a network may be compromised), but this is proof-of-concept work, the flaws found were fixed, and experts disagree on whether it is a new class of attack or a subclass of a known one.
summary: Ars Technica reports that independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin showed, in proof-of-concept tests on AI agents at organisations including Google, JPMorgan Chase and the US federal government, that a malicious instruction planted in one agent can be passed to other agents that trust it, using trust gaps in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that lets AI apps and agents communicate. Google and four other organisations have acknowledged such flaws in the past five months, and the Google flaw (rated 8 for severity) and a Rapid7 flaw (rated 2.7 out of 10) are fixed, but another researcher, Markus Vervier of the security firm X41 D-Sec, says the better label is prompt injection (hiding commands in text an AI reads), of which the technique is a simple subclass.
notes: Read in full. Date of the researcher's latest disclosure not stated by Ars; individual flaws were disclosed over the past five months. Related to the week's agent-security items (C12-12).
